title: Guests as Christ
hook: the Rule of Benedict: let all guests be received as Christ (Rule 53)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the infirmary: herbs by the sickroom, and books copied in the scriptorium. Your line was keepers of the light.

A knock at the monastery gate, after dark. Rain. On the other side of the door, a stranger: muddy boots, a wet cloak, nobody the porter has ever seen. Could be a pilgrim. Could be a thief. Could be a lord in disguise, or a beggar with nowhere else to go. The old porter gets up from his bench by the gate, and the words he's been taught come out first, before any question about who this is: thanks be to God.

The Rule of Benedict, the guidebook for monks from yesterday, has a chapter on guests, and it opens with a startling instruction: let every guest who comes be received as Christ. Why? Because, the Rule says, Christ himself will one day say the words of Matthew's Gospel, in the King James Bible: "I was a stranger, and ye took me in." So the stranger at the gate isn't an interruption. In the Rule's eyes, the stranger is Christ, arriving in disguise. And the chapter gets specific. The superior and the brothers go out to meet the guest. They pray together, then exchange the kiss of peace. The abbot pours water over the guest's hands, and he and the community wash the guest's feet. Visitors are fed. The Rule adds a line that's easy to miss: the poor and pilgrims are to be shown the most care, because in them Christ is received more especially. The rich, it notes dryly, get respect anyway, because people are wary of them. It's practical too. The abbot and the guests have their own kitchen, so people arriving at all hours don't disturb the brothers. Holiness with a spare kitchen. The first letter of Peter puts the same welcome in a few plain words: "Use hospitality one to another without grudging." Without grudging, even at the door after dark. The idea underneath doesn't need a monastery. Every door, sooner or later, has a stranger on the other side.
screen: `I WAS A STRANGER, AND YE TOOK ME IN.`

segments.voice: Think of the people who'll come to your door today, in person, on a screen, in your inbox: a coworker who always needs something, a delivery driver, a child who interrupts, someone you'd rather avoid. Choose one, and picture them arriving, and yourself standing up and going to meet them, glad they came. If you pray, pray for them by name; if you don't, just hold them in mind kindly.
Hospes. The Latin word for guest, and also host, in the Rule of Benedict's chapter that says every guest should be received as Christ.
Your line: receive them as christ. In the Rule, a knock is answered with thanks before any question. Day eight hundred forty-six, done.

howItsDone: Benedictine monasteries and convents keep guest houses where visitors can stay, pray with the community and share meals, and the porter or guest master greets them in the spirit of Rule 53.

chat.says: What does it mean that monks received every guest as Christ?
options: Benedict's Rule says Christ comes in the stranger, so every guest gets a real welcome.
Monks thought some guests might secretly be Jesus, so they checked who each one was.
Only important guests, like bishops and lords, were to be treated as Christ himself.

notes: Rule 53 paraphrased (no public-domain translation on the validator's list): guests received as Christ, citing Matthew 25:35; meeting the guest, prayer, then the kiss of peace; the abbot pours water on hands; abbot and community wash feet; special care for the poor and pilgrims; the rich get respect from fear of them (paraphrased as 'just by being rich'); a separate kitchen for abbot and guests. Confirm.
The porter's 'Deo gratias' on hearing a knock is from Rule 66, not 53; cited separately. Confirm.
'Benedictine monasteries still keep guest houses, and visitors of any faith or none still knock and are taken in': general, softened; confirm or cut under the claims rule.
Original: Latin hospes means both guest and host; the Rule's word for guests is hospites. Confirm the note.
Index hook cites 'Rule 53'; kept in the hook field.
